entities.name: Agapetus I
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pope Agapetus I, who served as the bishop of Rome from May 13, 535, until his death on April 22, 536, played a pivotal, albeit brief, role in the complex political and religious landscape of the early 6th century. Born into a distinguished Roman family – his father Gordianus was a priest, and he was likely related to Popes Felix III and Gregory I – Agapetus ascended to the papacy amidst the twilight of Ostrogothic rule in Italy and the burgeoning ambition of the Byzantine Emperor Justinian I. His pontificate is primarily defined by his courageous diplomatic mission to Constantinople, a desperate attempt to avert the Byzantine invasion of Italy and to address the escalating theological dispute over Monophysitism.

His most significant act was undertaking a perilous journey to Constantinople in 536, sent by the Ostrogothic King Theodahad to dissuade Emperor Justinian I from invading Italy. Although unsuccessful in preventing the Gothic War, Agapetus achieved a resounding theological victory. He refused to recognize the Monophysite Patriarch Anthimus I, who enjoyed the support of Empress Theodora, and after intense pressure and theological debate, Agapetus secured Anthimus's deposition. He then personally consecrated Menas as the new Patriarch of Constantinople, reaffirming the Chalcedonian Creed and temporarily strengthening the Roman See's doctrinal authority in the East.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Agapetus I's brief papacy significantly impacted the relationship between the Eastern and Western Churches by asserting papal authority in doctrinal matters, leading to the deposition of a patriarch in Constantinople and reinforcing Chalcedonian orthodoxy.
